references.text: The parallel passage in Matthew's Sermon on the Mount: 'No one can serve two masters. For he will hate the one and love the other, or be devoted to the one and despise the other. You cannot serve both God and Mammon' ([ref:Matt 6:24|Matthew 6:24]). This is almost word-for-word identical with Luke 16:13, but without the word 'slave' (οἰκέτης).

Joshua challenges the people to choose whom they will serve: 'Choose for yourselves this day whom you will serve' ([ref:Jos 24:15|Joshua 24:15]). The same basic principle: one must choose one master to serve; loyalty cannot be divided.

Elijah confronts the people on Mount Carmel: 'How long will you waver between two opinions? If the Lord is God, follow him! But if Baal is God, follow him!' ([ref:1 Kong 18:21|1 Kings 18:21]). Here too it is emphasized that one cannot serve two masters at the same time.

John warns against loving the world: 'Do not love the world… Whoever loves the world does not have the Father's love in them' ([ref:1 Joh 2:15-16|1 John 2:15–16]). Love for the world and love for God are mutually exclusive, just as service to God and Mammon.

James writes: 'Friendship with the world is enmity against God. Whoever wants to be a friend of the world becomes an enemy of God' ([ref:Jak 4:4|James 4:4]). This underscores the same principle as Jesus' words: one cannot serve two masters.

Paul warns that those who want to become rich fall into temptation and a trap: 'For the love of money is a root of all kinds of evil' ([ref:1 Tim 6:9-10|1 Timothy 6:9–10]). This highlights the danger of serving Mammon rather than God.

Paul writes that whoever you present yourselves as slaves to obey, you are slaves to that one whom you obey ([ref:Rom 6:16|Romans 6:16]). One cannot be a slave to two masters at the same time—either a slave to sin or to righteousness.

The immediate context in Luke: Jesus' teaching on using dishonest wealth wisely and about faithfulness in small things ([ref:Luk 16:9-12|Luke 16:9–12]). Verse 13 summarizes the lesson: ultimately, one cannot serve both God and riches.

During the temptation, Jesus rejects Satan's offer of worldly riches and says: 'Worship the Lord your God, and serve only him' ([ref:Matt 4:10|Matthew 4:10]). Jesus himself demonstrates the principle of serving God alone.

The psalmist warns: 'When wealth increases, do not set your heart on it' ([ref:Sal 62:11|Psalm 62:11]). Setting one's heart on riches is to make them one's master, contrary to wholehearted service to God.

Ecclesiastes writes: 'Whoever loves money never has enough; whoever loves wealth is never satisfied with their income' ([ref:Fork 5:9-10|Ecclesiastes 5:9–10]). Slavery to Mammon is insatiable and impossible to combine with service to God.
